description: Independent Instant Messages EN/C2 source-based test proposal; pending teacher approval.

tabs.title: Register and Interpretation
tabs.description: Analyse conventions that substitute for spoken context.

tabs.title: Audience and Evidence
tabs.description: Evaluate what survives when a message circulates.

questions.q: Why does the author resist treating informal spelling as evidence of deficient literacy?
choices: Instant messages never contain spelling mistakes.
Informal forms follow exactly the same rules as formal essays.
Readers can infer a writer's education from a single abbreviation.
A writer may deliberately choose a register suited to an intimate relationship.
questions.explanation: The opening uses 'u ok?' to illustrate purposeful register selection.

questions.q: How can repeated letters or punctuation function in written conversation?
choices: They guarantee a message is understood across cultures.
They help encode attitudes or rhythms that spoken language would signal differently.
They remove the possibility of misunderstanding.
They are merely decorations with no interpretive purpose.
questions.explanation: The author calls these conventions a repair kit for missing voices.

questions.q: What produces difficulties between a newcomer and an established messaging group?
choices: The newcomer may not share the group's implicit interpretive code.
The newcomer has necessarily written incorrect grammar.
Established groups are unable to learn new conventions.
Digital messages contain no tone under any circumstances.
questions.explanation: A shared code enables rapid interpretation, but newcomers may lack it.

questions.q: What does a screenshot preserve that can also make it misleading?
choices: The full history and relationships of all participants.
The exact voice tone used by the writer.
The words themselves, detached from the situation that shaped their meaning.
An unalterable record of the complete original conversation.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three contrasts preserved wording with discarded situational context.

questions.q: Why is the removal of laughing emojis significant in the invented class-chat example?
choices: It makes the remark grammatically incorrect.
It proves the student never intended to make a joke.
It changes the school rule being discussed.
It strips away cues that marked the original statement as exaggerated or ironic.
questions.explanation: The cropped image reaches the parent without signals supporting the intended ironic reading.

questions.q: Why does the author ask who bears responsibility for the controversy?
choices: There is one obvious person who is solely responsible.
The harmful outcome involves writing, selective cropping and uncritical forwarding.
The parent has the right to ignore missing context.
The first screenshot necessarily reveals the whole conversation.
questions.explanation: The questions distribute possible responsibility across multiple actors.

questions.q: What inconsistency does the writer identify in ordinary expectations of messaging?
choices: We always type slowly but read quickly.
Writers prefer written arguments while readers prefer photographs.
We compose messages like speech but interpret quoted messages like formal records.
Messages are deleted before anyone can quote them.
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph contrasts how messages are written and later judged.

questions.q: Why would deleting a message for everyone be insufficient protection?
choices: Copies may already have been saved or shared outside the original conversation.
Every app stores messages permanently in the open.
Recipients always ignore deleted messages.
Deletion automatically erases the context around the original.
questions.explanation: The writer notes that deletion cannot remove copies already made.

questions.q: What educational benefit comes from reconstructing the missing context of a screenshot?
choices: It guarantees that the original writer behaved responsibly.
It encourages inquiry before making a moral judgement.
It teaches students how to hide harmful content.
It eliminates every future misunderstanding.
questions.explanation: The classroom exercise turns quick condemnation into examination.

questions.q: What kind of literacy does the conclusion call for?
choices: A list of official abbreviations for all online communities.
A rule forbidding informal language in every school chat.
A guarantee that written messages will never be quoted.
An ability to ask who wrote a message, for whom and what has been omitted.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph defines sophisticated reading as reconstructing audience and context.
